signals: Shows genuine curiosity and willingness to learn
Can articulate what they did vs. what the team did
Demonstrates coachability and response to feedback
Shows basic ownership of small tasks or projects
Communicates clearly under light pressure
red_flags: Cannot describe a specific situation — only speaks in generalities
No evidence of initiative or self-starting behaviour
Blames others or circumstances without self-reflection
Unable to articulate what they personally contributed
Defensive or dismissive when probed
evaluation.seniority_note: Calibrate expectations to internship or early-career experience. Accept academic projects, extracurriculars, part-time work, and personal projects as valid evidence. Do not penalise for lack of professional experience. Focus on signal quality over story scale.

signals: Takes ownership of assigned work without constant prompting
Can describe how they worked through a technical or interpersonal challenge
Shows evidence of learning from mistakes
Collaborates effectively and contributes to team outcomes
Communicates blockers proactively
red_flags: Consistent passivity — always waiting to be told what to do
No examples of personal initiative or going beyond the brief
Blames team, manager, or environment for all setbacks
Cannot distinguish their contribution from the team's
Avoids specifics when pushed
evaluation.seniority_note: 1–3 years of experience expected. Accept both professional and project-based examples. Look for early ownership instincts and growth trajectory, not mastery. A strong junior shows a clear arc of improvement.

signals: Owns outcomes end-to-end, not just tasks
Has navigated cross-functional friction or competing priorities
Makes and defends technical or strategic decisions
Quantifies impact where possible
Shows upward influence — persuades, not just executes
red_flags: Still describes themselves primarily as a task-executor
Cannot give an example of influencing a decision or direction
Avoids conflict or difficult conversations rather than navigating them
No evidence of driving outcomes vs. contributing to them
Impact framing is entirely team-level with no personal thread
evaluation.seniority_note: 3–6 years expected. Look for evidence of growing scope — from task-level to outcome-level ownership. Strong mids have led something (project, initiative, technical decision) and can discuss the tradeoffs they made.

signals: Has shaped direction, not just executed against it
Drives outcomes across teams or functions
Comfortable navigating ambiguity and making calls without full information
Demonstrates investment in others' growth (mentorship, unblocking, sponsorship)
Impact is systemic — changes processes, norms, or culture, not just delivers projects
red_flags: Impact is still described at the individual-contribution level
No examples of influencing upward or across without formal authority
Struggles to describe ambiguous or underdefined situations they navigated
People development is absent from their narrative
Overly credits team for everything — ownership is unclear
evaluation.seniority_note: 6+ years expected. Senior candidates should demonstrate leverage — their work makes other people and systems more effective. Look for multiplier behaviours: mentorship, cross-functional influence, process improvement, and strategic input.

signals: Has driven org-level initiatives with multi-quarter scope
Aligns technical or operational work to business strategy
Communicates effectively to executives and non-technical stakeholders
Sets and enforces standards across teams or functions
Identifies and solves systemic problems before they become crises
red_flags: Impact is still described at the team level — no org-wide examples
Cannot describe how their work connected to business outcomes
Lacks examples of executive-level communication or influence
No evidence of standard-setting or culture shaping
Avoids or deflects questions about failure or hard tradeoffs at scale
evaluation.seniority_note: Staff-level candidates should demonstrate org-level leverage. They make engineering or operational orgs fundamentally more effective. Look for examples of systemic change, cross-org alignment, and business-level impact. Expect comfort discussing failure at scale.

signals: Can solve straightforward coding problems with guidance
Demonstrates basic understanding of time/space complexity
Writes readable, reasonably structured code
Communicates their thought process while solving
Asks clarifying questions before diving in
red_flags: Cannot produce working code for a simple problem
No awareness of edge cases or complexity
Silent while solving — does not communicate thinking
Defensive when given hints or directed corrections
Cannot explain their own code
evaluation.seniority_note: Intern-level technical bar is about potential, not mastery. Accept incomplete solutions that show correct thinking. Reward communication and curiosity over perfect code.

signals: Solves medium-difficulty problems independently
Handles edge cases without prompting
Writes clean, maintainable code
Can explain complexity and suggest optimisations
Shows debugging instincts when things break
red_flags: Needs significant hints to progress on medium problems
No edge case awareness
Cannot estimate or discuss complexity
Code is brittle or hard to follow
Cannot recover gracefully when stuck
evaluation.seniority_note: 1–3 years expected. Should solve medium problems reliably. Look for clean thinking, not just correct answers.

signals: Solves medium-hard problems with minimal prompting
Can design simple systems and discuss tradeoffs
Code is idiomatic and well-structured
Demonstrates good API and interface design instincts
Handles complexity and scale in their reasoning
red_flags: Cannot progress on hard problems without extensive hints
System design answers lack tradeoff reasoning
Code quality is inconsistent or unreliable
Cannot articulate design decisions
Freezes or shuts down under pressure
evaluation.seniority_note: 3–6 years expected. Should handle hard coding problems and basic system design. Look for design maturity and comfort reasoning about tradeoffs.

signals: Leads system design sessions with clear structure
Proactively identifies failure modes, scale bottlenecks, and tradeoffs
Can explain architectural decisions at multiple levels of abstraction
Writes or reviews production-quality code
Engages with ambiguity constructively
red_flags: System design is surface-level — no depth on tradeoffs or failure modes
Cannot drive the design without being prompted
Ignores non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability)
Code architecture is ad-hoc or monolithic
Cannot handle open-ended or ambiguous problems
evaluation.seniority_note: 6+ years expected. Senior technical interviews are largely system design. Expect candidates to drive, structure, and go deep. Coding should be near-production quality.

signals: Shows enthusiasm for learning technical and non-technical skills
Can describe a situation where they worked through a challenge
Communicates clearly when explaining their thinking
Shows basic initiative and curiosity
red_flags: Cannot give a single concrete example from any domain
Passive in both technical and behavioural responses
Defensive or disengaged under any pressure
evaluation.seniority_note: Intern-level mixed interviews combine light technical and basic behavioural. Expect academic or personal project examples. Focus on potential over polish.

signals: Shows ownership in both technical tasks and team situations
Can move between behavioural and technical contexts fluidly
Demonstrates early problem-solving instincts
Communicates proactively in both modes
red_flags: Strong in one mode (technical or behavioural) but absent in the other
Cannot connect their technical work to real impact
Avoids specifics in behavioural answers
evaluation.seniority_note: 1–3 years expected. Mixed junior interviews look for rounded capability — not a specialist yet, but shows instincts in both dimensions.

signals: Integrates technical and leadership thinking naturally
Can discuss both system-level tradeoffs and people/process decisions
Impact is demonstrable across both dimensions
Comfortable driving conversations in either direction
red_flags: Siloed — strong technically but avoids behavioural depth (or vice versa)
Cannot connect technical decisions to business outcomes
Leadership examples lack specificity or personal ownership
evaluation.seniority_note: 6+ years expected. Senior mixed candidates should demonstrate integrated thinking — where technical and leadership decisions compound each other.

signals: Can design a simple multi-service system
Identifies basic scaling and reliability concerns
Makes reasonable data modelling decisions
Communicates design clearly with diagrams or structured explanation
red_flags: Designs a monolith without considering tradeoffs
No discussion of data consistency or failure scenarios
Cannot structure the design conversation themselves
Ignores non-functional requirements
evaluation.seniority_note: 3–6 years expected. Expect medium-complexity systems. Probe for tradeoff awareness and structured thinking.

signals: Designs complex distributed systems with clear rationale
Proactively addresses failure modes, CAP theorem, and consistency tradeoffs
Scales the design incrementally with clear inflection points
Can go deep on any component without losing the overall picture
red_flags: Surface-level design — mentions components but cannot detail them
No discussion of failure, consistency, or operational concerns
Cannot handle scale or load follow-up questions
Loses the thread when pushed to go deep on a specific component
evaluation.seniority_note: 6+ years expected. Senior system design candidates should drive the session with minimal prompting. Expect depth on at least two major components.

signals: Approaches design from a platform and ecosystem perspective
Discusses multi-system integration and dependency management
Makes strategic technology choices aligned to org constraints and future state
Addresses operational maturity — observability, incident response, runbooks
Can articulate the build-vs-buy-vs-adopt spectrum with nuance
red_flags: Designs in isolation — no consideration of org constraints or existing systems
Cannot speak to operational reality of running the system at scale
Technology choices are arbitrary or fashion-driven rather than principled
Does not consider migration path from current state to future state
Cannot engage at the strategic/executive level when pushed
evaluation.seniority_note: Staff-level system design is about platform and ecosystem thinking. Expect candidates to reason about org constraints, migration paths, and the strategic rationale behind architecture decisions — not just technical correctness.
